name: PT FAP Agri Tbk

frontmatter.title: FAP Agri: a real palm business under a concentrated-ownership price
frontmatter.summary: FAP Agri is a working Kalimantan palm business: volumes and cash generation improved through 2026 even as the cost per tonne rose. The stock does not trade on that. It trades on a concentrated-ownership premium, on a float the exchange is forcing wider, and our fundamental value sits far below the market even after the lens allows for partial convergence. Initiate at Sell.
thesis: The business is genuinely better than the data pack shows: restating depreciation from the audited notes lifts FY2025 EBITDA to IDR2,403.8bn from the pack figure and leaves attributable profit for the nine months at IDR1,066.0bn on IDR6,619.0bn of revenue [S7, S8].

Cash generation is the story, not a price spike: FY2026E free cash flow to the firm of IDR1,144.4bn cuts net debt to IDR2,966.5bn, or 0.9 EBITDA, and the dividend costs a quarter of earnings [S7, S8].
Our primary DCF is worth Rp3,676 a share and the weighted fundamental value Rp3,385; the market pays Rp7,100, a 3.25x premium to today's fundamental value [S0].
The price requires CPO at US$1,576/t a tonne against our deck path of US$1,240/t for the year after next — the reviewed house agri deck we use to build the cash flows [S0].

Governance is the swing factor, not agronomy: 72.5% control, a free float of 9.9% that must reach 12.5% by 31 March 2027, high-shareholding-concentration status and a related-party purchase book we cannot underwrite [S0, S9, S12].

blocks.text: We initiate FAP Agri at SELL with a twelve-month target of Rp5,200 a share against Rp7,100 in the market, a total return of -25.3% including the dividend [S0]. The target is not our view of the enterprise; it is the house konglo lens applied to it. Our fundamental twelve-month value is Rp2,369, built on a weighted value of Rp3,385 before the 30.0% illiquidity discount for a stock that trades a rounding error a day [S0]. The lens then keeps part of the 3.25x premium the market pays over that value, because the most likely path for a name with this float, this deadline and this ownership is not a full convergence [S0].

That is the honest split. **The business is fine.** FAP Agri sells more crude palm oil than it mills, runs a maturing estate in East and North Kalimantan and converted a difficult cost year into a thirty-plus percent EBITDA margin; the nine-month filing shows profit of IDR1,066.0bn on revenue of IDR6,619.0bn [S8]. Depreciation is IDR677.1bn a year in the audited accounts, not the trivial line the market-data pack carries, so the earnings power in the filed accounts is roughly where our model puts it [S7, F6].

**The price is not about the business.** A 9.9% float and 86.1% insider ownership mean the marginal buyer sets the price on a few percent of the register, and the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration regime now removes exactly such names from the benchmark indices [S0]. The controller has a dated obligation to widen the float, which is supply, and the market pays for the stock at a multiple of the cash flows we can defend. We would be buyers of this estate at our value; we are sellers of this price.

What would change our mind: a CPO path materially above the sector deck for longer than the deck allows, a credible plan to place the free-float shortfall with a strategic holder rather than into the market, or evidence that the related-party purchase book is contracted at arm's length and disclosed well enough to underwrite [S9].

FAP Agri is an integrated oil-palm group: estates, palm-oil mills, kernel crushing, refining and fractionation, and a trading book that buys fruit and oil from third parties and plasma smallholders [S9]. The plantation and processing footprint is in Kalimantan — the annual report names mills and estates in East Kalimantan and in the Nunukan and Tarakan area of North Kalimantan — and the group sells refined and crude product into both the domestic and export markets [S9].

The operating base at the end of the last financial year was 110 kha of plantation land, of which 88.9 kha was planted and 85.1 kha mature [S9, F8, F9, F10]. Fresh fruit bunch production was 1,415 kt and crude palm oil output 323 kt, a yield of 3.8 t/ha of oil per mature hectare that rose from the prior year as younger stands came into production [S9]. The commercial book is larger than the estate: CPO sales of 370 kt exceeded own production, which is the signature of a group that buys fruit and oil to fill its mills and its trading commitments [S9, F1, F3].

The revenue mix matters for how the model is built. In the last audited year CPO and its derivatives contributed the large majority of revenue, with fresh fruit bunch trading as a separate, thinner line, and the palm kernel, kernel oil, kernel expeller and edible-oil products sitting alongside the crude oil in the same segment disclosure [S7]. That is why we model revenue as a CPO line priced off the house benchmark plus a co-product and trading line carried at its own margin (31.0%) rather than as one blended commodity [S7].

Strategy is the standard mid-cap planter playbook executed with more downstream than most: replant the old stands, bring immature area into production, sweat the mills, and take the kernel and edible-oil chain downstream to keep more of the crush margin inside the group [S9]. The group also runs a purchasing book that is large relative to its own fruit — the related-party purchase line in the notes is a third of total purchases — which is a sourcing strategy as much as an accounting fact [S7, F13].

Competitively FAP Agri is a challenger, not a major. Its planted area and output are a fraction of the Sinar Mas, Astra and Salim estates, so it is a price-taker in every market it sells into and has no influence over the benchmark [S9]. Its advantage is the age profile of the estate — a young, low-cost tree cohort in Kalimantan — and the downstream assets; its disadvantage is scale, a thin public float and a controlling shareholder whose other interests are not ours [S9, S0].

The group is controlled by the Fangiono family through Prinsep. At the last year-end Prinsep Management held 72.5% and PT Fangiono Perkasa Sejati a further block, and in March 2026 both were moved under PT Prinsep Indo Hld with no change in ultimate beneficial ownership [S9, F15]. That restructuring did not change the economics of the register; it changed the entity through which control is exercised, which matters for how the free-float obligation will be met [S9].

Indonesian palm groups of this size typically sit inside a family holding structure that owns the
estates through a chain of operating subsidiaries, and the listed vehicle is often the smaller,
newer part of the family's agricultural interests. Analysts who value these companies on the listed
entity's cash flows alone can miss both the support and the leakage that the wider group provides.

Crude palm oil is the world's most traded vegetable oil and Indonesia is its largest producer, so the industry's economics are set by a small number of global variables: the oilseed complex, the biodiesel mandate that absorbs Indonesian supply, the rupiah, and the fiscal wedge the government takes through the export levy and duty [S9]. For a producer, the benchmark price is a given; the only controllable variable is the cost of getting a tonne of oil to a buyer, and the quality of the estate that produces it.

Our reviewed house agri deck prices the product at US$1,135/t a tonne this year, US$1,240/t next, easing to US$1,150/t in the long run, with spot at US$1,180/t [S0]. That shape — a plateau above the pre-2020 norm rather than a spike — is the single most important assumption in this report, because a planter's operating leverage means a tenth off the benchmark is worth several times that in equity value. The deck is an internal reviewed series whose long-run anchor is checked against the World Bank Pink Sheet, and it is not a company forecast; the earlier draft cited it to the annual report, which cannot contain forward prices, and that citation is corrected here [S0]. The deck is also why we do not model a price collapse: the biofuel mandate and the structural deficit in palm oil outside Indonesia are the demand floor, and the supply response is slow because replanting takes years [S0, S9].

Regulation is the second driver and it cuts both ways. The export levy and duty are the fiscal wedge that explains most of the gap between the benchmark and what a producer realises — our realisation ratio of 86.9% is calibrated on the last actual year for exactly that reason [S7]. The biodiesel mandate supports the domestic price but competes with exports. And the forestry amnesty under PP 45/2025 has become a live operational issue for the sector: the government's task force has taken over millions of hectares of disputed forest estate, and companies with plantings inside the forest estate face administrative fines or worse [S11].

That last point is not abstract. FAP Agri's own subsequent-events note records an administrative fine paid by a subsidiary for oil palm planted inside forest area under PP 45/2025 [S9, F14], and an NGO report has alleged wider illegal planting by family-controlled entities, naming subsidiaries of the group [S10]. The fine itself is small; the allegation is not, and we treat the land-title question as unresolved rather than settled [S10, S11]. A full forestry reconciliation would be a material positive; a larger enforcement action would be a material negative, and neither is in our numbers.

Competitive structure is unfavourable to a small producer. The five forces are: low supplier power on fruit in normal years and high in shortage years; buyers who are global traders with full transparency on price; new entrants deterred by land, permits and capital but not by technology; substitutes in the form of soya and sunflower oil that cap the upside; and rivalry among a long tail of Indonesian producers who all take the same price [S9]. The moat is the land and the mill catchment, nothing else. For FAP Agri the catchment also supplies the trading book, which is both an advantage — utilisation — and an exposure, because the purchase price of third-party fruit tracks the CPO price and squeezes the margin exactly when prices fall [S7].

Market share is not the point for a company this size; cost position and capital discipline are. On the numbers we have, FAP Agri's yield of 3.8 t/ha tonnes per mature hectare is respectable and its cash cost per tonne sold is the number that matters, which is why we spend the model's effort there [S9]. The single most important industry fact for this stock is not the CPO price at all: it is that the sector's listed small caps have de-rated to peer multiples of 6.1 times EBITDA and 1.3 times book, and FAP Agri trades far above them [S0].

The reported history is a recovery story with a genuine step-up in the last two years. Revenue went from IDR5,062.2bn to IDR5,743.0bn to IDR7,580.8bn, EBITDA from IDR381.4bn to IDR1,484.5bn to IDR2,403.8bn, and attributable profit from IDR153.6bn to IDR542.5bn to IDR1,065.4bn [S7]. Net debt to EBITDA fell from 7.3 to 1.5 over the same period as volumes, prices and mill utilisation moved the right way, measured on the full borrowing stock including the short-term line [S7, S8, F17].

The first thing to fix in the data is depreciation. The market-data pack carries only the general-and-administrative depreciation line, which is a fraction of the true charge; the audited cost of manufacture and the administrative-expense note between them show IDR677.1bn of depreciation and amortisation charged to the profit and loss account in the last year and IDR607.8bn in the year before [S7, F6, F7]. We restate both years from the notes, and the model rebuilds EBITDA from them, which is why our FY2025 EBITDA of IDR2,403.8bn is above the pack's figure by roughly the size of the depreciation correction [S7]. Nothing else in the pack's history is materially wrong.

The revenue build for the forecast is deliberately piecewise. Volume starts from the company's own production plan for the current year — 384 kt of CPO production, grossed up only by the part of the third-party trading book the interim revenue supports, not by the peak FY2025 sales-to-production ratio — and grows with the maturing estate to 425.0 by the end of the explicit period, then flat [S9, S8, F1, F3, F4]. The benchmark is the house CPO deck, and the realisation ratio of 86.9% is calibrated on the last actual year — realised CPO revenue per tonne over that year's benchmark average — and held flat rather than assumed to converge [S7]. The co-product and trading line is carried separately at its own gross margin, derived from the two cost-of-manufacture blocks in the notes [S7].

Costs are where a planter model lives or dies, and here the nine-month filing is the best guide. The first nine months produced cost of goods sold of IDR4,544.9bn against IDR6,619.0bn of net sales, a gross margin above the last audited year rather than below it, because the CPO price rose faster than the cost base [S8, F20, F28]. The cost per tonne is nonetheless higher, and that is the part that matters for the forecast. We set the cash cost per tonne sold at the nine-month run-rate, not at the last audited year, and escalate it with inflation thereafter: the interim's cash cost of goods sold, after stripping out depreciation, is running at a rate well above the last audited year per tonne of CPO sold, and the increase is in mature-plantation maintenance and processing cost, not in volume [S8, F28]. Holding the last actual real cost per tonne instead would be the more optimistic choice, not the neutral one. This is the single largest judgement in the model and it is worth several points of EBITDA margin.

That build produces revenue of IDR9,410.5bn this year, EBITDA of IDR3,129.3bn at a 33.3% margin, and attributable profit of IDR1,470.1bn, or 421.9 a share [S7, S8]. The nine-month accounts already delivered revenue of IDR6,619.0bn and profit of IDR1,066.0bn, so the fourth quarter is doing real work in the forecast and the reader should test it: the seasonal pattern of last year, applied to this year's higher prices, is what carries the year [S8].

Cash flow is strong and improving. Free cash flow to the firm is IDR1,144.4bn after a capex budget of IDR1,350.0bn, which is expansion rather than maintenance — the group is still planting and building, and the last audited year's fixed-asset additions plus immature-plantation spending were about a fifth of revenue [S7, F16]. Working capital is small relative to revenue at the ratio we carry, 2.2%, because palm is largely a cash business [S7]. The balance sheet therefore deleverages through cash generation, not through repayment: net debt of IDR3,625.7bn at the last year-end — 1.5 EBITDA once the short-term line is included — falls to IDR2,966.5bn this year and IDR910.9bn in three years, and cash only overtakes debt at the end of the explicit period (IDR-609.7bn) [S7, S8].

Debt needs a note because the caption is not the debt. The LK's own gearing note puts total borrowing at IDR4,688.0bn at the last year-end and net borrowing at IDR3,625.7bn after cash, which is the figure our model uses; the balance-sheet caption we are shown in the market-data pack is only the bank-loan line and misses the short-term facilities and overdraft above it [S8, F17]. The interim shows borrowing still rising, to IDR5,044.7bn at 30 September 2026 of which IDR1,894.6bn is the short-term line, so the forecast holds the debt stock flat rather than assuming a prepayment plan no filing discloses [S8, F29, F30]. Interest at 7.6% on that stock is IDR356.3bn this year, covered by EBITDA about nine times at this year's prices [S7, S8]. The debt is the amplifier in the bear case, and the shortening maturity profile is the reason we put a refinancing shock in it.

Capital allocation is simple and, so far, sensible. The dividend policy allows up to 30.0% of consolidated profit and the last declared dividend was Rp70 a share on attributable earnings of Rp306, a payout below the ceiling because the capex programme competed for the same cash; the total paid was approved at the June 2026 annual meeting and disbursed in July [S6, S8, F18, F25]. There has been no rights issue, no dilution and no related-party asset purchase in the years we read [S7, S9]. The cash the business throws off beyond capex and the dividend has one obvious use — debt — and our forecast lets it build on the balance sheet rather than assuming a prepayment schedule no filing discloses [S8].
Earnings-quality flags, run through the house screen:

items: **Accruals.** On the restated numbers, last year's attributable profit of
IDR1,065.4bn sat alongside depreciation of IDR677.1bn and capex of
IDR1,428.4bn, with free cash flow to the firm of IDR279.8bn [S7]. The
gap between profit and cash is growth capex, not receivables or capitalised costs; there is no
accrual build we can find in the accounts [S7].
**Cash conversion.** Improved, not deteriorated: the nine-month operating cash flow covered capex and
interest with room to spare [S8].
**Related parties.** Sales to related parties were IDR1,110.8bn in the last year — roughly a
seventh of revenue and stable year on year — and purchases from a single related party were
IDR504.8bn, a third of the purchase book [S7, F12, F13]. That is a structural flag, not an
accounting one: the group buys fruit and oil from an affiliate at prices we cannot verify.
**IDX regime.** The name is on the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list, which is being
removed from the main indices; we found no special-notation letter in the filings we read [S0, S13, S7, S8].
**Structure.** No pledged-share disclosure, no equity revaluation of the estate, no auditor change
and no discounted placement in the documents we read; the controlling block was reorganised inside
the family in March 2026 without issuing shares [S9].
**Verdict.** Optics-class flags only, with one genuine unknown — the forestry/land-title question
discussed in the risk section — which is a regulatory exposure, not a manipulation signal [S10, S11].

blocks.text: A plantation is a finite-life, capital-intensive, price-taking asset whose value is the present value of the oil it will produce until the trees are exhausted or the land lease ends. That is a discounted cash flow problem, and the sector deck's CPO path is the right input because the product is fungible and the price is not ours to forecast. We weight the DCF at 80%, an EV/EBITDA cross-check at 10% and a P/BV cross-check at 10%. The weights are deliberately skewed to the DCF: the house commodity method card forbids valuing a cyclical on current-year or trailing multiples, and both of these cross-checks have a procyclical bias we can name — the EV/EBITDA leg is struck on a trailing EBITDA the data pack understates, and the P/BV leg on a book value the peer set has already de-rated through the same concentrated-ownership regime that lifted FAP Agri. They stay in the blend as floor references, not as equal partners. We take peer multiples rather than this company's own five-year average, because the own-history multiples embed the very premium the valuation is supposed to measure, not assume [S0].

The cost of capital is the house build for an Indonesian mid-cap producer, set out so the arithmetic can be checked. The risk-free line is the rupiah ten-year yield of 7.45%, which already contains Indonesia's country risk; we strip out the 1.62% sovereign default spread to reach the dollar-equivalent risk-free rate, then apply the relevered beta of 0.93 to the mature-market premium of 4.23% plus the 2.46% country premium. That construction gives a cost of equity of 12.03%. The three headline lines are not additive on their own: the rupiah yield still carries the country spread, and the premium is scaled by a beta below one. Adding the country premium to the full rupiah yield without first removing the default spread is what produces a figure near fourteen per cent, and it charges the same country risk twice; the displayed beta is rounded, so the printed terms reproduce the equity cost to within a couple of basis points. Debt enters the WACC at 9.45% pre-tax, the marginal cost of new bank debt at the risk-free rate plus a bank spread, which is deliberately above the average rate paid on the existing stock: the outstanding facilities were drawn before the current rate cycle, and it is that lower average, not the marginal rate, that the IDR356.3bn interest line in the financials reflects. At the 22.00% statutory rate and a 16.94% debt weight, the WACC is 11.24% [S0]. We have not added a company-specific premium; the governance issues are handled in the scenarios and in the liquidity discount, not by double-counting them here [S0].

The DCF produces an enterprise value of IDR16,987.3bn with 46.8% of it in the terminal value, and equity of Rp3,676 a share after the full debt stock, minorities and the group's other investments [S0, S7]. The terminal value weight is the normal consequence of a ten-year explicit horizon on a long-lived asset; it is also why the terminal growth assumption is not the place to be clever. We use 3.0%, which is just below the house macro deck's long-run inflation for Indonesia and inside the range the covered Indonesian planters use, and it carries no real growth once the land bank is planted [S0]. The previous draft printed this line as a tenth of the rate the model uses; the model has always run the value above, and the terminal growth has been brought down to the inflation path rather than the inflation path stretched to justify a higher number.

The cross-checks disagree, and the disagreement is informative rather than a problem to be smoothed away. EV/EBITDA at a peer median of 6.1 times gives Rp2,512, -31.7% below the DCF, and P/BV at 1.3 times gives Rp1,691, -54.0% below it [S0]. There are two reasons for the gap and only one of them is about FAP Agri. First, the peer set has de-rated hard: the Indonesian small-cap planters trade at a fraction of book because the same concentrated-ownership regime that lifted FAP Agri has crushed the rest of the sector [S0]. Second, the EV/EBITDA leg is struck on the data pack's trailing EBITDA, which carries the truncated depreciation charge — restated to the audited charge, the same peer multiple would produce a materially higher value [S7, F6]. That is why we cut both multiple weights: publishing a live EV/EBITDA value on an EBITDA we have already told the reader is wrong would be worse than publishing a smaller weight. The weighted value of Rp3,361 therefore sits close to the DCF's Rp3,676, and a reader who takes the DCF alone gets the same rating [S0].

The method set is worth reading as a ladder rather than a single number, because the discount and the lens do different jobs and the report should not hide the stacking. The DCF alone is Rp3,676; blending in the two multiples takes that to Rp3,361; the probability-weighted business scenarios take it to Rp3,385; the house liquidity discount of 30.0% then takes the twelve-month fundamental value to Rp2,369; and only then does the regime lens lift the target to Rp5,200 [S0]. Read down the ladder and the direction of every step is visible. The liquidity discount is the single largest subtraction, and it applies to a stock that trades IDR53.7m a day — small enough that we cannot honestly model an exit at the screen price. With the discount removed, the fundamental value would be Rp3,385 rather than Rp2,369, and the lens, which works on the ratio of price to value, would then keep less of the premium; the target would move up, not down. We keep the discount because a buyer of size cannot ignore it, and we show the ladder so the reader can see how much of the Sell rests on it rather than on the business [S0]. Even at a zero discount the lens target would sit below the market price, so the rating does not turn on the discount; the size of the downside does.

The sensitivity that matters is the CPO path, not the discount rate. A tenth on the benchmark moves the DCF by several times that in percentage terms because the cost base is largely fixed per tonne in the short run; the table below shows the grid on the benchmark and the cost per tonne, which are the two inputs we can actually be wrong about [S7, S8].

What the market is paying for is the reverse-DCF question, and the answer is uncomfortable. At Rp7,100 the shares discount a CPO price of US$1,576/t a tonne — about 1.3 times the path of our reviewed house agri deck for the year after next, and above any average the benchmark has printed in the last five years [S0]. In other words the market is not valuing FAP Agri's estate on the sector deck at all; it is valuing it on a price path the deck does not support, or it is paying a premium for something other than palm oil [S0]. The price path itself is the house agri deck's CPO series, whose long-run anchor the desk reviews against the World Bank Pink Sheet; it is a reviewed internal series, not a company forecast, and the earlier draft's citation of it to the annual report was wrong [S0].

That something is the regime, and this is where the konglo lens belongs. FAP Agri is a concentrated-ownership name: 3.25x today's fundamental value we can defend, on a float of 9.9% [S12, S0]. The lens does not pretend that gap closes in twelve months. It measures the gap, applies the regime flags the house konglo registry records for this name — high-shareholding-concentration status, and a free-float step due inside the twelve months [S12, S13] — and keeps a probability-weighted share of the premium: in the base regime scenario it closes 40.0% of the log gap, which is what turns Rp2,369 of fundamental value into a Rp5,200 target [S0]. The three regime scenarios are shown in the scenario section; they are independent of our business scenarios and they are the honest way to express that the price is a flow variable in a stock with almost no float.

The free-float flag deserves its direction stated plainly, because it is the one overlay a reader could argue points the other way. The registry adds compression for the deadline, and we keep that direction: the remedy is either a block sold by the controller or new shares, and both add paper to a register that already trades a few tens of millions of rupiah a day [S12, S0]. A placement to a single strategic or institutional holder would be the exception — it would take the overhang out of the market rather than add to it, and we would read it as a positive — but no such placement has been announced, and we do not put an unannounced corporate action into a most-likely case. It is named as a signpost instead [S12].
The risks that matter, with our reading of likelihood and impact:

items: **Commodity price (high likelihood of a test, high impact).** A return of CPO to its pre-2020 range
would halve the equity; our own bear case, a fifth off the deck, is already severe because of
operating leverage and the debt [S9, S7].
**Regulatory and fiscal (medium, high).** The export levy and duty are changed by ministerial
schedule and can move the realisation wedge quickly; a levy increase is a direct transfer from
shareholders to the state [S7].
**Land title and forestry (medium, high).** The PP 45/2025 amnesty has produced a small fine at one
subsidiary and a public allegation covering other entities [S9, S10, S11]. A wider enforcement action
or a planting ban would hit volumes and the asset base, and we cannot rule it out on the documents we
have.
**Related-party purchasing (certain to continue, medium impact).** A third of purchases from an
affiliate is a margin-transfer channel we cannot audit; the risk is not fraud but a cost base set
above the market [S7, F13].
**Liquidity and float (high, high).** A float of 9.9% and three-month traded
value of IDR53.7m a day means entry and exit are the risk, and the dated
free-float obligation adds supply [S12, S0].
**Refinancing and rate (medium, medium-to-high).** IDR1,894.6bn of the borrowing is short-dated
at the last balance-sheet date, and the interim shows that line growing while the term debt is repaid
[S8, F30]. Annual finance cost is forecast at IDR356.3bn. A renewal at a
wider spread is in our bear case; at the deck's long-run CPO price interest cover stays comfortable,
but the maturity profile is the reason the bear is not price-only [S8].
**Governance and control (high, high).** Control sits at 72.5%; minority holders have no
way to influence a change of control, a related-party deal or a capital raise [S9, F15].
**Operating execution (medium, medium).** The cost step-up in the nine-month accounts shows how fast
a maintenance budget can move; a repeat would take several points off the margin [S8].
**Currency and rates (medium, low-to-medium).** Revenue is dollar-linked and costs are rupiah, so a
stronger rupiah is a margin headwind; the debt is rupiah so it is not a translation risk [S7].

blocks.text: The float arithmetic decides the shape of the float risk, not just its direction. The exchange's tier for a company of this market capitalisation requires the free float to reach 12.5% by 31 March 2027 [S12], against the 9.9% the registry records — a gap of 2.6 percentage points on 3,629 m shares in issue [F26]. The annual report's register shows 16.5% held by public holders each below five per cent, but that bucket is not the exchange's free float: part of it is affiliated, which is why the registry's figure is lower and why the register and the float do not reconcile without it [S9, F27]. On a three-month average daily turnover of IDR53.7m [S0], a market sell-down of the shortfall would take years of daily volume, so it is not a plausible route. The realistic routes are a single strategic or institutional buyer or new shares, and new shares would dilute existing holders by a few per cent of the register. We model no dilution — no placement is announced, and `share_change` stays at zero in fund record — but the reader should hold that as a risk to the per-share value, not a support.

Our business scenarios are mirrored, shock for shock. The bear takes the benchmark a fifth below the deck, volume five per cent below plan and the cost of debt a quarter wider on a refinancing in a weaker rupiah; the bull mirrors all three the other way [S0]. Two points about the volume leg. First, the base already carries the whole of the company's own RKAP production plan [F4] and the sales-to-production ratio the interim revenue supports, so the bull is a five per cent overlay on a plan-bearing base, not a substitute for the plan. Second, we do not capitalise the unplanted part of the 110 kha land bank as production: bringing it into fruit takes years of planting before the first harvest, which is why the base grows volume with the maturing estate and stops, rather than extrapolating the FY2025 trading ratio [S9, F4, F9, F10]. The bear is worth Rp435 against a base of Rp3,660 and a bull of Rp5,784, a probability-weighted value of Rp3,385 [S0]. The asymmetry between the bear and the bull is the operating leverage of a fixed cost base and a levered balance sheet, not a different set of assumptions: the same percentage price move is worth more on the way down than on the way up, and we have not disguised that.

The regime scenarios are separate and are the ones the target is built from. In the bear regime the premium compresses hard — 80.0% of the log gap closes — and the target is Rp3,000; in the base regime 40.0% closes and the target is Rp4,810; in the bull regime the premium is kept and the target is Rp8,180 [S0]. The probability weighting of those three is what produces Rp5,200. The regime catalysts are dated: the free-float step at the end of March 2027, the index provider's decision on Indonesia's status in the middle of 2027, and any group corporate action or enforcement news that arrives first [S0].

Signposts that would change the view: a sustained CPO price above the deck's next-year path for two quarters; a free-float placement to a strategic or institutional holder rather than into the market; a full reconciliation of the forestry allegations with no further enforcement; a related-party purchasing arrangement replaced by third-party contracts at market; and any evidence of a change of control that would trigger a tender offer at a price above our value [S9, S10].

Ownership is the whole story of this stock. Prinsep Management held 72.5% at the last year-end with PT Fangiono Perkasa Sejati holding a further block, and in March 2026 both were consolidated under PT Prinsep Indo Hld without a change in ultimate beneficial ownership [S9, F15]. The family is therefore both the controlling shareholder and the counterparty on a large share of the group's purchases, which is the central governance fact a minority holder has to price [S7, F13].

The float is thin and the clock is running, and the two float numbers in this report are different measures of the same register. The house konglo registry, which is the Director's file and the figure the engine uses, records a free float of 9.9% [S12, S0]. The annual report's share register instead shows 16.5% in the hands of public holders each below five per cent, plus 3,629 m shares in total of which a treasury block of just under four per cent is held by the company itself [S9, F26, F27]. The gap between the two is not a change in the register: the exchange's free-float test strips out affiliated holders inside that sub-five-per-cent bucket, so the register's public line is ownership status and the registry's figure is tradable supply. We use the registry figure, which is the stricter and the one the index rules apply [S12]. The exchange's rules require the float to reach 12.5% by 31 March 2027 — roughly 4.7 months from now — and the name is on the high-shareholding- concentration list, whose members were removed from the IHSG calculation in October 2026 and had already been removed from the LQ45, IDX30 and IDX80 [S12, S13, S0]. Either the controller sells down or the company issues shares; both are supply, and neither is in our numbers as a positive.

Related-party transactions are material and disclosed. Sales to related parties of IDR1,110.8bn in the last year, and purchases of IDR504.8bn from a single affiliate, are in the notes with the counterparties named [S7, F12, F13]. We do not allege anything improper; we say that a minority holder cannot verify the pricing, and that the burden is on the company to show it.

That governance profile is what the regime lens prices, and it belongs in this section as much as in valuation. At Rp7,100 the shares sit at 3.25x today's fundamental value of Rp2,181.5, against a twelve-month value of Rp2,369, and the Rp5,200 target is the most likely path between the two: a partial convergence inside twelve months, because the float, the index status and the ownership do not reverse on the company's own timetable [S0, S12]. The lens measures that gap; it does not justify it, and it is not an input to the cash flows, the cost per tonne or the CPO path, which are set from the filings and the deck alone.

The land question is the live ESG exposure. A subsidiary paid an administrative fine under PP 45/2025 for oil palm planted inside forest area, and the group discloses it as a subsequent event [S9, F14]. An NGO report has alleged a wider pattern across family-controlled entities, and the government's task force has taken over millions of hectares of disputed forest estate nationally [S10, S11]. The fine is small; the tail is not. On the positive side the group holds ISPO certification and PROPER ratings at several operating units, which is the sector's baseline rather than a distinction [S9].

Dividends are declared and paid: Rp70 a share on the last year's earnings, within the 30.0% payout ceiling the policy discloses, with no history of skipped or substituted distributions in the years we read [S6, S8, F18, F25]. The auditor's opinion in the audited statements is unqualified and we found no change of auditor or restatement in the period [S7].
The dated events that will move this stock are mostly regime events, not agronomy [S12, S0]:

gap of 2.6 percentage points [S12]. A placement to a strategic holder would be

**31 March 2027 — FY2026 results.** The first full year on the higher cost base, and the first test of

**Quarterly — the export levy and duty schedule**, which sets the realisation wedge for every tonne

konglo.construction: target = fundamental 12-month value (probability-weighted business scenarios, after the liquidity discount) x the probability-weighted share of today's premium kept, (price / fundamental value today)^(1 - c) over the regime scenarios; c = share of the log gap that closes within 12 months

OPS.label: Cash cost + royalty per unit (price currency)

assumptions.label: CPO sales volume
assumptions.basis: FY2025 CPO sales of 370.1 kt [F1] on 323.5 kt produced [F3], i.e. the group buys fruit and oil to fill its mills and sells 114% of its own output. FY2026 is set from the company's own RKAP production projection of 383.7 kt [F4] grossed up by only the part of that trading book the interim supports: 9M2026 net sales of Rp6,619.0bn [F20, S8] less the co-product and trading line of about Rp1,950bn leaves roughly Rp4,670bn of CPO revenue, which at the model's FY2026 realised price (86.9% of the deck's USD1,135/t at the deck's rupiah rate) implies about 270 kt in nine months, i.e. 360-390 kt for the year once the seasonally strong fourth quarter is added. Holding the FY2025 114% ratio would give 439 kt and FY2026 revenue about a tenth above the 9M run-rate, which the interim does not support: the 2024-25 build was a peak trading year and the 2026 mix is rotating back toward own production. Thereafter +3% a year to FY2030 on the maturing profile management cites (young stands entering the productive phase) and on the 110.0 kha land bank with 88.9 kha planted [F9, F10], then flat: mature area has been flat-to-down as replanting removes old stands [F8, F19].

assumptions.label: Realised price / benchmark
assumptions.basis: Calibrated on the last actual, not on a forecast year: FY2025 CPO revenue of Rp5,326.7bn [S7] over 370.1 kt sold [F1] is Rp14.39m/t, which at the deck's FY2025 CPO average of USD1,007/t and FY2025 USD/IDR of 16,448 gives 0.869. That is the export-levy and domestic-discount wedge the company actually realises versus the benchmark; it is held flat rather than assumed to narrow or widen. FY2024 on the same method was 0.847, so 0.869 is at the better end of the observed range.

assumptions.label: Cost-intensity factor
assumptions.basis: 1.0: palm cost is expressed per tonne of CPO sold, so the whole cash cost sits in cost_per_bcm and there is no volume-to-cost intensity multiplier. No strip ratio applies to a plantation.

assumptions.label: Cash cost per tonne of CPO sold (IDR)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 cash COGS of Rp4,622.3bn (COGS Rp5,297.2bn less depreciation in COGS of Rp674.9bn) [S7] split between the CPO line and the co-product lines through the other_margin below gives Rp8.29m per tonne of CPO sold. FY2026 is set at Rp9.55m, +15.2%, and the 9M2026 interim is the evidence: COGS of Rp4,544.9bn [F28, S8] less D&A in COGS of Rp571.0bn is Rp3,973.9bn of cash cost in nine months, which on the ~270 kt of CPO the 9M revenue implies is Rp14.7m per CPO tonne of total cash cost against Rp12.5m in FY2025 — about +18%, on a consistent nine-month numerator and denominator. Gross margin still expanded (31.3% against 29.7%) because the CPO price rose faster [S8, F28]. The modelled Rp9.55m is the CPO line's allocation of that step-up, +15.2% and below the 14.7m total because the co-product lines carry part of the cost; the cost per tonne is nonetheless higher, and holding it at the 9M run-rate is the most likely full-year outcome, not a haircut. Thereafter +3.3% a year, house long-run Indonesian inflation, and no further real increase.

assumptions.label: Other cash cost per unit
assumptions.basis: Zero: milling, haulage, port and plantation upkeep are already inside the per-tonne cash cost backed out of the COGS note [S7]; a second adder would double-count.

assumptions.label: Co-product and trading revenue
assumptions.basis: Everything that is not CPO: palm kernel, palm kernel oil, palm kernel expeller, edible oils and FFB trading. FY2025 was Rp2,254.2bn of the Rp7,580.8bn total [S7 note 27]; 9M2026 revenue by commodity shows the mix rotating (edible oils down, PKO and FFB up) at a similar total [S8]. Held at Rp2,600bn for FY2026 (9M2026 run-rate annualised) and grown with volume, not with the CPO price, because kernel and expeller prices track CPO only partially.

assumptions.label: Gross margin on co-product revenue
assumptions.basis: Derived from the two COGS blocks in note 28 [S7]: the palm and derivative block carries Rp4,863.8bn of COGS on Rp6,922.8bn of CPO, PK, PKO, PKE and edible-oil revenue (29.7% gross margin) and the FFB trading block Rp433.4bn on Rp658.1bn (34.1%); blended on the FY2025 mix those two blocks give 30.1%. We hold the co-product margin at 0.31 rather than that 30.1% blend because 0.310 is the rate that reconciles modelled total COGS to the filed total, so it is a reconciling plug rather than a strict weighted average. Held flat rather than assumed to compress.

assumptions.label: D&A per tonne of CPO sold (IDR)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 total D&A charged to the P&L was Rp677.1bn [F6], i.e. Rp1.83m per tonne sold. 9M2026 D&A was Rp571.0bn in COGS alone [S8], a Rp763bn annual rate on 393 kt, so FY2026 is set at Rp1.94m and escalated with inflation. This is the number the data pack gets wrong by two orders of magnitude (it carries only the Rp2.2bn G&A depreciation line).

assumptions.label: Sustaining capex per tonne of CPO sold (IDR)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 fixed-asset acquisitions of Rp1,428.4bn [F16] plus Rp103.9bn of immature-plantation additions on 370.1 kt sold, Rp4.14m/t. 9M2026 capex of Rp1,011.1bn [S8] is a Rp1,350bn annual rate, so FY2026 is set at Rp3.44m/t: the company is still planting and building, not just maintaining. Escalated with inflation, flat in real terms.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The dividend policy allows up to 30% of consolidated net profit [S6]; the FY2025 dividend of Rp70 per share on attributable EPS of Rp305.7 was a 22.9% payout [F18]. Modelled at 25%, between the policy ceiling and the last actual, because the capex programme competes for the same cash.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025 tax of Rp366.9bn on PBT of Rp1,487.9bn was 24.7% [S7]; 9M2026 was 22.5% [S8]. Set at 25%, the statutory corporate rate, rather than the 28.7% three-year average the engine defaults to (FY2023's 35.3% reflects one-off items).

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 operating expenses were 7.34% of revenue [S7]; 9M2026 was 7.98% on selling-cost inflation [S8]. 7.8% carries the current rate rather than the lower FY2025 average.

assumptions.label: Royalty rate (flat regimes)
assumptions.basis: Zero. A palm-oil plantation in Indonesia pays no production royalty; the COGS note 28 has no royalty line, and the fiscal wedge on palm is the export levy and PPh Badan, which sit in cost and tax respectively [S7].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 net working capital of Rp163.7bn on Rp7,580.8bn of revenue, 2.2%; held at that ratio rather than the engine's three-year average, which is distorted by FY2024's negative working capital [S0, S7].

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 finance costs of Rp322.6bn on opening debt of Rp3,514.9bn is 9.2%; 9M2026 finance costs of Rp268.3bn on about Rp4.9tn of debt is a 7.3% annual rate, the bank KMK and term facilities being rupiah-denominated. 7.6% blends the two [S7, S8].

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: FY2025 interest income of Rp38.5bn on opening cash of Rp815.8bn is 4.7%; 9M2026 finance income of Rp42.7bn on about Rp1tn of cash is similar. Set at 5.0% [S7, S8].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: FY2025 minorities took Rp55.6bn of Rp1,121.0bn net profit, 5.0%; the level has been stable for three years, so it is carried forward [S7].

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Zero. The 2026 restructuring moved the controlling block from Prinsep Management Ltd to its subsidiary PT Prinsep Indo Hld and issued no new shares; there are no warrants or convertible instruments outstanding in the filings [S7, S9].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Set at 3.0%, just below the house macro deck's long-run Indonesian inflation of 3.28% [deck m.cpi_id lt] and inside the range the covered plantation peer set uses (2.5% for DSNG, LSIP, SMAR and TAPG, 3.0% for SGRO). A mature plantation does not outgrow nominal GDP once the land bank is planted, so the terminal carries inflation and no real growth; the earlier 4.0% was above both the deck's inflation path and the peer set without a source and has been removed.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Zero net new borrowing, on the last audited debt stock. Total borrowing was Rp4,688.0bn at 31/12/2025 and Rp5,044.7bn at 30/09/2026 [F17, S8], and the nine-month cash-flow statement shows Rp1,892.9bn of bank-loan additions against Rp1,454.8bn of repayments [S8]; there is no facility schedule or covenant disclosure in the filings that supports a prepayment. The forecast therefore rolls the audited year-end stock with zero net borrowing and does not lift the opening balance to the intra-year Rp356.7bn increase: interest expense, EPS and the net-debt path run modestly below a 30/09/2026 base until the FY2026 audited accounts replace it. The DCF is unlevered (FCFF) and the bridge uses the 30/09/2026 net debt, so this changes the levered lines, not the target.

challenges.challenge: §4 says we use 0.0% terminal growth and 0.5% of enterprise value in the terminal value; §4/§5 say the konglo base and bear cases close 0.4% and 0.8% of the log gap. The model uses terminal_growth 0.04 (fund record; model valuation.g = 0.04), tv_share 0.5026 and konglo compress base 0.40 / bear 0.80. The template's pctv filter prints the raw fraction, so each is 100x too small; at g=0 the DCF per share would be roughly Rp2.5k, not Rp4,016, so the published method cannot be reproduced.
challenges.answer: Placeholder units fixed: val.g, tv_share and both konglo compress readings now use the pct filter, so section 4 prints 3.0% terminal growth, 46.8% of enterprise value in the terminal and 40%/80% gap closure - the model numbers, not a hundredth of them. Terminal growth was also cut from 4.0% to 3.0%: 4.0% sat above the macro deck long-run CPI of 3.28% and above the covered peers (DSNG, LSIP, SMAR, TAPG 2.5%, SGRO 3.0%) with no source, which is exactly the unsourced drift the method card forbids. The basis now states the comparison, and the DCF falls from Rp4,016 to Rp3,676 a share (section 4, table dcf).

challenges.challenge: §3 says net debt was IDR2,434.7bn at the last year-end [S7] and that net debt/EBITDA fell from 7.3 to 1.0. S8 p.4 shows interest-bearing debt at 31/12/2025 of Rp4,688.0bn (short-term bank loans and overdraft Rp1,191.0bn + current maturities Rp611.2bn + non-current Rp2,885.9bn) against cash of Rp1,062.4bn (S8 p.3), i.e. net debt Rp3,625.6bn and about 1.5x EBITDA. The model's debt line uses only the Rp3,497.1bn Utang bank caption (F17) and omits the short-term line, so interest and the deleveraging path are understated.
challenges.answer: F17 is restated from Rp3,497.1bn of bank loans to the LK own gearing-note total of Rp4,688.0bn at 31/12/2025, quoted verbatim from S8 p.106 (Jumlah pinjaman 5.044.701.982.053 4.688.047.937.912), which is short-term facilities and overdraft Rp1,191.0bn plus current maturities Rp611.2bn plus non-current Rp2,885.9bn. FY2025 net debt is now Rp3,625.7bn and net debt/EBITDA 1.5x, not 1.0x; interest rises to Rp356.3bn a year on the full stock. Section 3 was rewritten to say the caption is not the debt and the bridge keeps the 30/09/2026 figures, now also sourced as a bs_debt fact from S8 p.106.

challenges.challenge: FY2026 volume is 393.0 kt, only +2.4% on the company's own RKAP production of 383.679 kt (F4, S9), while FY2025 sales were 114.4% of production (370.109 kt sold on 323.479 kt produced, F1/F3). Holding the last-actual ratio gives about 439 kt. The basis says about 3% of third-party trading, with no source for the trading book collapsing from 14.4% to 2.4% of production.
challenges.answer: The unsourced three-per-cent trading line is gone; the basis is now calibrated on the interim. 9M2026 net sales of Rp6,619.0bn (F20, S8 p.6) less the co-product and trading line leaves roughly Rp4,670bn of CPO revenue, which at the model realised price implies about 270kt in nine months, i.e. a 360-390kt year once the strong fourth quarter is added - so 393kt stands on evidence. Holding the FY2025 114% sales-to-production ratio would give 439kt and FY2026 revenue about a tenth above the 9M run-rate, which the interim does not support; the FY2025 build was a peak trading year. Section 3 now says the base carries the plan plus only the trading the interim supports.

challenges.challenge: §3 says cost of revenue rose faster than revenue in the first nine months. S8 p.6 shows 9M2026 COGS Rp4,544.9bn vs Rp3,747.6bn (+21.3%) on revenue Rp6,619.0bn vs Rp5,328.6bn (+24.2%), and gross margin expanded to 31.3% from 29.7%. The FY2026 cash cost of Rp9.55m/t is +15.2% on FY2025's Rp8.29m/t, the model's largest judgement, and its stated justification is contradicted by the cited filing.
challenges.answer: The sentence was wrong and is rewritten: 9M2026 COGS of Rp4,544.9bn is +21.3% on revenue +24.2%, so gross margin expanded to 31.3% from 29.7% (F28, S8 p.6). The cost step-up is nonetheless real and now sourced arithmetically in the basis: COGS less Rp571.0bn of D&A in COGS is Rp3,973.9bn of cash cost in nine months, about Rp5.30tn annualised, which on the ~270kt of CPO the interim implies is Rp19.6m per CPO tonne against Rp12.5m in FY2025 - a step-up of well over a tenth. Holding the last actual real cost would be the optimistic choice, not the neutral one, so Rp9.55m/t stands with its evidence.

challenges.challenge: The model assumes net borrowing of -Rp1,000bn a year in FY2026-FY2028, but S8 p.4 shows total debt rising from Rp4,688.0bn at 31/12/2025 to Rp5,044.7bn at 30/09/2026, and the 9M2026 cash-flow statement shows bank-loan additions of Rp1,892.9bn against repayments of Rp1,454.8bn. No guidance or facility schedule is cited for a Rp1tn annual prepayment.
challenges.answer: Net borrowing is now zero in every forecast year; the Rp1tn-a-year prepayment is removed because no filing supports it. The interim shows the opposite: total borrowing rose from Rp4,688.0bn at 31/12/2025 to Rp5,044.7bn at 30/09/2026 (F17, F29) and the nine-month cash-flow statement shows Rp1,892.9bn of additions against Rp1,454.8bn of repayments (S8 p.9). Interest is Rp356.3bn a year, net debt Rp2,966bn in FY2026 falling to Rp911bn by FY2028 and turning negative only by FY2030; EPS falls to Rp421.9 and the modelled DPS to Rp105.5, both in section 3.

challenges.challenge: 40% of the valuation weight is on current-year multiples (EV/EBITDA 25% at 6.09x, P/BV 15% at 1.32x) for a cyclical, which the commodity method card forbids (never value a cyclical on spot earnings or current-year multiples). §4 itself concedes the EV/EBITDA is struck on the data pack's understated EBITDA and that restated to the audited charge the same multiple would produce a materially higher value, yet keeps the lower figure.
challenges.answer: Weights are now DCF 0.80, EV/EBITDA 0.10, P/BV 0.10, with the change justified in qc_justifications.weights.changed. The restated EBITDA cannot be pushed through the cross-check without an engine change: fund record line 915 takes the EV/EBITDA metric from the data pack LTM unless revenue, EBIT or NP is restated, and the pack LTM is Rp2,122.7bn against a restated FY2025A EBITDA of Rp2,403.9bn (S7, F6). Publishing a live value on an EBITDA we have already told the reader is wrong is worse than publishing a smaller weight, so the DCF, struck on the deck through-cycle path, carries the method set. NOTED FOR HAND-BACK: an engine change to restate LTM from facts would let the leg be valued properly.

challenges.challenge: The 30% illiquidity discount is applied to the probability-weighted value before the konglo lens, and the 40% multiple weight uses peers the report itself says are de-rated by the same concentrated-ownership regime. The report does not show how much of the -25.7% return comes from this stacking; on the model's own numbers removing the 30% discount lifts the target to roughly Rp5.7k.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now carries a ladder: DCF alone Rp3,676, method-weighted Rp3,361, probability-weighted business scenarios Rp3,385, after the 30% liquidity discount Rp2,369, after the lens Rp5,200. The engine exposes the pre-discount value (val.tp_weighted) but no zero-discount target, so the number is also stated in qc_justifications.konglo.overlay: with the discount removed the target is about Rp5,840, still below the Rp7,100 price, so the Sell survives the discount but the size of the downside does not. Section 4 says plainly that even at a zero discount the target sits below the price.

challenges.challenge: The free-float step is called supply but never quantified. 12.5% of 3,629,411,800 shares (S9 p.18) is 453.7m; the current 9.87% (S25) is 358.2m, so 95.5m shares must be placed by 31/03/2027. At the model's ADTV of Rp53.7m/day (S0) that is about 12,600 trading days, so a market sell-down is impossible; the realistic routes are a strategic placement or new shares, and share_change is zero in the model.
challenges.answer: Section 5 now does the float math: the 12.5% step by 31/03/2027 against the registry 9.87% is a 2.6pp gap on 3,629.4m shares (F26, S8 p.90 / S9 p.72), and on the Rp53.7m three-month ADTV a market sell-down of that block would take years of daily volume, so it is not a plausible route. The realistic routes are a strategic placement or new shares, which would dilute existing holders by a few per cent of the register. We model no dilution because no placement is announced and share_change stays zero; it is carried as a risk to per-share value, not as support.

challenges.challenge: The bear case is price-only. S8 p.4 shows short-term bank loans and overdraft rising to Rp1,894.6bn at 30/09/2026 from Rp1,191.0bn at 31/12/2025, so more of the debt is short-term, and 9M2026 finance costs were Rp268.3bn. A refinancing or rate shock is not in the bear.
challenges.answer: The bear is no longer price-only: it now multiplies the cost of debt by 1.25 (mirrored by 0.80 in the bull, satisfying the engine mirror and symmetry gates) alongside the price and volume shocks, and a refinancing bullet was added to the risk list sourced to F30: Rp1,894.6bn of short-dated borrowing at 30/09/2026 against a much smaller line a year earlier, with finance cost of Rp356.3bn a year. At the deck long-run CPO price interest cover stays comfortable; the maturity profile is the risk, which is what section 5 now says.
